729.title: Abu Bakr, as-Siddiq
729.hook: Abu Bakr believes without hesitation and brings others: Uthman, Talhah, Zubayr, Abd al-Rahman, Sa'd
729.howItsDone: Sunni Muslims know Abu Bakr as as-Siddiq, say 'may Allah be pleased with him' after his name, and honor him as the first caliph; Shia Muslims read the succession after the Prophet differently. His early belief is retold in sirah study.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the first to believe. Khadijah, Ali, Zayd and Abu Bakr, the people who knew him best. Your line was: first to believe.

Some answers take weeks. Others come before the question is finished. In Ibn Ishaq's sirah, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, is remembered as saying that everyone he invited to Islam hesitated, held back, thought it over, except one man. When he told Abu Bakr, Abu Bakr did not hold back and did not hesitate. A merchant of Quraysh, well known and well liked, a man people came to with their business and their questions. He hears it, and says yes. Today: Abu Bakr.

His title is as-Siddiq. Tradition explains it through sidq, truthfulness: a siddiq is someone who confirms the truth, who takes a true word as true. There's a hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari, from a later quarrel among the companions, where the Prophet defends him with a memory: when he was sent, people said, you are lying, and Abu Bakr said, he has spoken the truth, and stood by him with himself and his wealth. That is what the name holds. Sirah writers also tell that the title stuck after the Night Journey, when Abu Bakr was told the Prophet claimed to have gone to Jerusalem and back in a night, and answered that if he said it, it was true. That story belongs later in the year. Abu Bakr didn't keep his yes to himself. Ibn Ishaq names the men who came to Islam through him: Uthman ibn Affan, az-Zubayr ibn al-Awwam, Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf, Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, and Talhah ibn Ubaydullah, names that will come back again and again. He brought them to the Prophet, and they believed. How? Ibn Ishaq describes him as a man people liked to sit with, who knew the genealogies of Quraysh, easy and kind in company. His friends trusted him, so they listened. The same quality that made him believe at once made others willing to hear.

730.title: The house of al-Arqam
730.hook: early Muslims meet in secret at a young man's house to learn and pray
730.howItsDone: Muslims remember Dar al-Arqam in sirah study as the house where the early believers met to learn and pray; Muslims still gather in small study circles to learn the Qur'an together.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Abu Bakr, as-Siddiq, who believed at once and brought his friends. Your line was: he believed at once.

A door near the hill of Safa, in the middle of Mecca. People come to it one at a time, not in a crowd: a merchant, a freed slave, a young man from a powerful clan. Inside, someone is reciting new verses slowly, so they can be learned by heart. Others are bowing in prayer. Outside, the city goes about its business, and the door stays shut. Today: Dar al-Arqam.
screen: `A DOOR NEAR SAFA.` → `ONE AT A TIME.` → `VERSES LEARNED BY HEART.`

segments.voice: Al-Arqam ibn Abi al-Arqam was one of the early believers, from the clan of Makhzum, and the sirah writers describe him as young when he came to Islam. He had a house near Safa, and he opened it. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, used it as a meeting place for the believers: a place to teach, to recite what had come down, and to pray together out of sight. Why out of sight? The sirah tells that the early Muslims at first went out to the valleys around Mecca to pray, and that at least once they were found there and mocked, and it came to blows. A house was safer. So for a stretch of time, this small house became something like a hidden school. Look at who could sit together there. Outside, in Mecca, a person's clan decided much of how they were treated. Inside al-Arqam's house, a freed man and a merchant of Quraysh could sit in the same room and learn the same verses from the same teacher. Sirah writers later called it Dar al-Arqam, the house of al-Arqam, and some of them tell of people who came to Islam within its walls. And what made it possible was one young man saying, use my house. He didn't preach in the street. He offered a room near Safa, with a door that could be shut.

731.title: Three years quietly
731.hook: for about three years the call is private, person to person
731.howItsDone: In sirah study Muslims divide the Meccan call into a private stage and a public stage, and the early private stage is often discussed as a model of patient, personal invitation.

segments.voice: Yesterday: al-Arqam, whose house near Safa became a hidden school. Your line was: a hidden school.

No speeches. No crowd gathered at the hill. For a long stretch at the beginning, the message in Mecca travels the way a family recipe travels: one person leans toward another and says, come, let me tell you something. A friend to a friend. A brother to a sister. A master's household to a servant. Ibn Ishaq, the early biographer, gives this quiet season a length. Today: Ibn Ishaq.
screen: `NO SPEECHES. NO CROWDS.` → `ONE PERSON TO ANOTHER.` → `A QUIET SEASON.`

segments.voice: Ibn Ishaq writes that three years passed between the time the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, kept his message private and the time he was commanded to make it public. Some other writers count the time differently, so hold the number loosely; the shape is what the sirah keeps. First quietly, then openly. What did quiet look like? The last few days of this path: Khadijah in the house, Ali and Zayd at the table, Abu Bakr bringing his friends one conversation at a time, prayer in the valleys, then behind al-Arqam's door. People heard it from someone they already knew, face to face, with time for questions. Why begin that way? The sources don't give one reason, and readers offer several. Some point to protection: a small group was easy to crush. Some point to teaching: the first believers needed time to learn the verses and pray together before anything was asked of them in public. Some simply notice that this is how trust moves, from someone you know. Then the season ends. The Qur'an gives a command that Pickthall translates: "So proclaim that which thou art commanded." And another verse tells him to warn his nearest kin. What he does with that command is tomorrow's story. Today is the quiet before it, and the quiet was not empty. It built the people who would stand beside him.

732.title: The call from Safa
732.hook: he climbs Safa and asks, would you believe me if I said an army was behind this hill
732.howItsDone: Muslims retell the call from Safa as the beginning of the public message in Mecca; pilgrims on Hajj and Umrah walk between Safa and Marwah, though that rite remembers Hajar, not this day.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ibn Ishaq, and three quiet years of one person telling another. Your line was: quietly first.

Ya sabahah! The cry goes up from the little hill of Safa. It's the alarm call, the one people shout when raiders are coming at dawn. Men drop what they're doing and come running; those who can't come send someone to find out. The clans of Quraysh gather at the foot of the hill and look up. Standing on top is the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him. The quiet season is over. Today: nadhir.
screen: `A CRY FROM THE HILL.` → `THE CLANS COME RUNNING.` → `THE QUIET SEASON IS OVER.`

segments.voice: Sahih al-Bukhari keeps the scene from Ibn Abbas. When the verse came, warn thy nearest kin, he climbed Safa and called the clans by name. When they had gathered, he began not with a sermon but with a question. If I told you that horsemen in the valley were about to attack you, would you believe me? They answered: yes, we have only ever known you to tell the truth. Then he said: I am a warner to you, before a severe punishment. Look at how he builds it. He lets the city testify to his honesty before he says a single new thing. Years of trust, from the market, from the black stone, from Khadijah's caravans, are called in with one question. And the word he uses for himself is nadhir, a warner. Not a ruler, not a fortune-teller. Someone who has seen what's coming and shouts so others can get ready, the way the alarm call itself works. It is a word the Qur'an also uses for him. The report also says that one voice in the crowd answered him with a curse. Who it was, and what came back, is tomorrow. Today, hold the question: would you believe me? It asks what kind of life makes a person believable when it matters.

733.title: The uncle who cursed
733.hook: Abu Lahab curses him in front of all, and Surah al-Masad answers
733.tomorrow: The sun in my right hand
733.howItsDone: Surah al-Masad (111) is a short surah that Muslims memorize and can recite in prayer; its occasion, Abu Lahab's words at Safa, is taught alongside it in tafsir and sirah study.

segments.voice: Yesterday: nadhir, a warner. He asked the clans at Safa, would you believe me, and they said yes. Your line was: would you believe me?

Back at the foot of Safa. The clans have just said, we have only known you to tell the truth. He has just called himself a warner, before a severe punishment. Some of them had left their work to come. Then a voice cuts across the crowd. Not a stranger's voice. His own uncle's. Al-Bukhari keeps the words in Ibn Abbas's report: may you perish, was it for this that you gathered us? Today: Abu Lahab.
screen: `THE CROWD AT SAFA.` → `A VOICE CUTS ACROSS IT.` → `HIS OWN UNCLE.`

segments.voice: He's known as Abu Lahab. That's a kunya, a 'father of' name, and tradition reads it as father of flame; the sources give his given name as Abd al-Uzza. He was a son of Abd al-Muttalib, a brother of the Prophet's father, and he lived close by. Family. That is what makes the moment sting. The report in al-Bukhari says that after his words, a surah came down: surah one hundred eleven, al-Masad, the palm fiber. Pickthall translates its first verse: "The power of Abu Lahab will perish, and he will perish." The surah goes on to say his wealth will not help him, and it speaks of his wife carrying firewood, with a rope of palm fiber around her neck, which gives the surah its name. The tradition reads it as Allah's answer, not as a nephew trading insults with his uncle. And look at what is missing from the scene. On Safa, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, is not reported to curse back. In the tradition's reading, the reply is the surah. A small hadith in al-Bukhari shows the same habit later. Quraysh took to calling him Mudhammam, the blamed one, a twist on Muhammad, the praised one. He said to his companions: doesn't it amaze you how Allah turns their insults away from me? They curse Mudhammam, and I am Muhammad. The insult missed. A curse came at him in public, from family, and he didn't answer it with another.
screen: `ABU LAHAB, HIS UNCLE.` · `SURAH AL-MASAD ANSWERS.` · `HE DOES NOT CURSE BACK.` · `THEY CURSE MUDHAMMAM.` · then, large: `THE POWER OF ABU LAHAB WILL PERISH.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one sharp word someone threw at you, maybe from family; you don't have to forgive it right now, or pretend it didn't hurt. Just practice not throwing one back, even in your head: each time a reply rises, breathe out and let it drop. If you pray, you can leave the matter with Allah.
Abu Lahab. The uncle who answered the call from Safa with a curse, and the surah al-Masad that came down in reply. Today's word.
Your line: let it go. An insult aimed at Mudhammam can miss its mark. See you tomorrow.

734.title: The sun in my right hand
734.hook: the sirah tells of his answer to Quraysh's offers: even if they put the sun in one hand and the moon in the other, he would not stop
734.howItsDone: Muslims retell the sun-and-moon answer in sermons and sirah classes as a picture of steadfastness under pressure; scholars of hadith discuss how strongly the report is transmitted.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Abu Lahab, the uncle who cursed, and a nephew who didn't curse back. Your line was: let it go.

What would it take? That's the question the leaders of Quraysh start asking once the message is public. The sirah says they try offers: money, if he wants money; honor, if he wants honor; leadership, a crown even. And if it's some sickness, they'll pay for a healer. It's a generous list. They also try pressure, on the man who protects him: his uncle. Today: Fussilat.
screen: `WHAT WOULD IT TAKE?` → `MONEY, HONOR, A CROWN.` → `PRESSURE ON HIS UNCLE.`

segments.voice: This story comes to us through the sirah, from Ibn Ishaq. The elders of Quraysh go to Abu Talib and press him: stop your nephew, or step aside and let us deal with him. Abu Talib is shaken. He calls the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, and in effect says: spare me, and spare yourself; don't put on me more than I can carry. And the nephew answers with the line that names today. As Ibn Ishaq tells it: O my uncle, by Allah, if they put the sun in my right hand and the moon in my left, on condition that I give this up, I would not give it up until Allah makes it prevail or I die in the attempt. Then, Ibn Ishaq says, he wept, and got up to leave. Not gold, not a kingdom: the sun and the moon. The offer isn't refused because it's too small. It's refused because the thing he carries isn't for sale at any size. The sirah keeps another version of the offers too, where a Qurayshi leader named Utbah comes himself with the list, and the Prophet answers by reciting from the Qur'an, from the surah later called Fussilat, until Utbah goes back to his people looking changed. Two scenes, one answer. And notice the tears. This is not a hard man enjoying a refusal; it costs him to say no to his uncle. What Abu Talib says next is tomorrow.

segments.voice: Ask yourself what's offered to you, small or large, to let go of something you care about: a shortcut at work, a little gossip to fit in, comfort in place of honesty. Hold your hands open on your lap, palms up, feel the weight of the offer, and then quietly turn your palms down. If you pray, ask Allah for steadiness.

735.title: Abu Talib's shield
735.hook: his uncle never accepts Islam, yet protects him to the end
735.howItsDone: Muslims remember Abu Talib's protection of the Prophet in sirah study; Sunni and Shia Muslims differ on his faith, and both speak of his loyalty with honor.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Fussilat, and a nephew who refused even the sun and the moon. Your line was: the sun in my hand.

We left a nephew in tears, getting up to leave his uncle's house. He has just refused the sun and the moon. His uncle has just asked him to spare them both. Now Abu Talib calls him back. He has every reason to step aside: the leaders of his own tribe are angry with him. Ibn Ishaq gives his words: go, son of my brother, and say what you like; by Allah, I will never hand you over. Today: Banu Hashim.
screen: `THE NEPHEW, IN TEARS.` → `THE UNCLE CALLS HIM BACK.` → `I WILL NEVER HAND YOU OVER.`

segments.voice: Abu Talib had taken the boy in after his grandfather died, and raised him with his own children, Ali among them. As the sirah tells it, Abu Talib stood at the head of the Banu Hashim, and while he stood behind his nephew, Quraysh could not simply take him. Quraysh tried to get around it. The sirah tells of a strange offer: they brought him a handsome young man of their own, Umarah ibn al-Walid, and said, take him as your son, and hand us your nephew. Abu Talib's answer, in Ibn Ishaq: you give me your son to feed, and I give you mine to kill? He refused. Then comes the question of his own faith. In Sunni sources, including al-Bukhari, Abu Talib is reported to have died without accepting Islam. Shia tradition holds that he was a believer who kept it hidden to protect his nephew. The two readings differ, and both remember him with honor for what he did. Either way, the outward story is the same: a man who did not publicly follow the message stood between it and harm, at a cost to his standing among his own people. This week has been about people around the Prophet: Abu Bakr believing at once, al-Arqam opening his house, the quiet season, Safa, the uncle who cursed. Two uncles, two sons of Abd al-Muttalib. One cursed him in front of the clans. The other said: I will never hand you over.
